lesson.title: Increasing and Decreasing Analysis: Building the Sign Chart
lesson.summary: A sign chart for f' turns the list of critical numbers, including the ones where the derivative simply does not exist, into a complete map of exactly where a curve climbs and where it falls.
lesson.body:
The standard method for increasing and decreasing analysis is a sign chart: find every critical number, mark those numbers on a number line, and test the sign of f' in each resulting interval. A critical number is any x in the domain of f where f'(x) = 0 or where f'(x) fails to exist. That second category, points where the derivative is undefined, is easy to forget, but skipping it can hide a real local extremum that a plain "solve f'(x) = 0" search would never catch.

Start with the familiar case. Let f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x. Then f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3), zero at x = 1 and x = 3. Testing each interval: for x < 1, both factors (x - 1) and (x - 3) are negative, so their product is positive, giving f' > 0; for 1 < x < 3, (x - 1) is positive and (x - 3) is negative, giving f' < 0; for x > 3, both factors are positive, giving f' > 0 again. So f increases on (-infinity, 1), decreases on (1, 3), and increases on (3, infinity), with a local maximum at x = 1 (f(1) = 1 - 6 + 9 = 4) and a local minimum at x = 3 (f(3) = 27 - 54 + 27 = 0). That is the ordinary case, entirely built from solving f'(x) = 0.

Now consider a function where the derivative itself breaks down at a critical point. Let f(x) = x^(2/3). This function is defined for every real number, since it can be written as (x^(1/3))^2, and a cube root is defined for negative inputs too. Its derivative is f'(x) = (2/3)x^(-1/3) = 2/(3x^(1/3)), which is undefined at x = 0, since that would require dividing by zero, even though f(0) = 0 is perfectly well defined. So x = 0 is a critical number, not because f'(x) = 0 there, but because f' simply does not exist there.

Building the sign chart around it: for x > 0, x^(1/3) is positive, so f'(x) is positive; for x < 0, x^(1/3) is negative, so f'(x) is negative. The sign of f' changes from negative to positive at x = 0, so the First Derivative Test applies exactly as it would at an ordinary critical point, confirming a local minimum at x = 0, with value f(0) = 0. But the character of that minimum is different from the smooth minimum in the previous example: as x approaches 0 from the left, x^(1/3) approaches 0 through negative values, so f'(x) = 2/(3x^(1/3)) plunges to negative infinity, and as x approaches 0 from the right, f'(x) climbs to positive infinity. The tangent line is effectively vertical on both sides, producing a sharp point, a cusp, at the minimum rather than a smoothly rounded bottom.

This function is also even, since (-x)^(2/3) = ((-x)^(1/3))^2 = (-(x^(1/3)))^2 = (x^(1/3))^2 = x^(2/3) = f(x), so the decreasing branch for x < 0 is a mirror image of the increasing branch for x > 0, both branches meeting at the sharp minimum on the axis of symmetry. The lesson of this example is the reason increasing and decreasing analysis names both categories of critical number explicitly: a sign chart built only from solving f'(x) = 0 would have missed x = 0 entirely, since that equation has no solution there, and would have concluded, wrongly, that f never changes from decreasing to increasing at all.
